full_judgment:
Muhammad Ansar Ali, J: It appears that this appeal has been filed on behalf of accused appellant Md. Abul Kalam under Section 30 of the Special Powers Act 1974 against an order dated 8.6.1994 passed by the learned Sessions Judge, Satkhira though designated as Senior Special Tribunal in the cause title of the petition of this appeal rejecting an application for bail of the appellant in Crl. Misc. Case no. 167 of 1994 arising out of G.R. Case No. 71 of 1994 i.e. Satkhira P.S. Case No. 23 dated 15.2.1994 under section 25B of the Special Powers Act for alleged recovery of Bangladeshi currency notes and American Dollar from the accused. From the impugned order it further appears that the learned Sessions Judge did not consider the merit of the application for bail of the appellant as still then there was no charge sheet submitted for any offence under the Special Powers Act 1974 by the investigating officer in the instant case but he somehow rejected the prayer for bail of the appellant. As against the order of rejection of the prayer for bail, the present appeal has been preferred by the appellant Md. Abul Kalam in this court which is now taken up for hearing. 

 4. From a perusal of the above provision of the Special Powers Act it is clear that unless an order is passed by the Special Tribunal no appeal lies under Section 30 of the Special Powers Act in this Court. In the instant case at the time of passing the impugned order there was no charge-sheet filed in the case and as such the Sessions Judge could not and did not act as a Special Tribunal to take cognizance of the offence as alleged and as such he could not entertain the application for bail as a Special Tribunal and in the instant case he heard the application as a Sessions Judge and passed the impugned order of rejection of bail of the appellant not as Special Tribunal but as Sessions Judge. Hence we find that from the impugned order rejecting the prayer for bail, no appeal lies under Section 30 of the Special Powers Act in this court. In that view of the matter the appeal is found to be not maintainable and as such it is dismissed on the ground of non maintainability. 

 5. Mr. Abdul Quayum the learned Advocate for the appellant however could not refute the above proposition of law but he submits that the application for bail before the learned Sessions Judge was filed under Section 32 of the Special Powers Act and as such he passed the order as Special Tribunal, though it does not appear from the impugned order that he passed the order as Special Tribunal. Mr. Quayum also tried to argue that 2 of the accused persons namely Abdur Rashid and Abul Kalam Bhuiyan had been enlarged on bail in an application under Section 498 of the Code of Criminal Procedure by a division bench of this court and that the case of the appellant is on a better footing and as such the accused appellant should have been granted bail as the alleged offence under Section 25 B of the Special Powers Act is not attracted in the facts and circumstances of the case. 

 6. No one appears for the State in this appeal. But we have considered the maintainability of the appeal as stated above ourselves after hearing the appellant's Advocate and have come to the above conclusion but as to the merit of the case of the appellant for bail, in view of our above decision, we cannot and don't like to make any observation or finding the point raised by the learned Advocate for the appellant as to the non-attraction of the alleged offence under Section 25(B) of the Special Powers Act may be argued before the trial Court at the hearing of the case and so far the prayer for bail of the accused appellant, if so advised, he may file a fresh application for bail before the trial court stating all necessary facts and the trial-court may be pleased to consider such application for bail in the facts and circumstances of the case seeing that no discrimination is made in the matter of bail.
